final_text: A 1 TB file holds 10^12 bytes, but a 4-byte integer only reaches about 2.1 billion (signed) or 4.3 billion (unsigned). Byte offsets into the file must therefore be 64-bit (8-byte) integers. With 8-byte offsets the 170,000-word index is still only a few MB.
note: Oracle Java tutorial: int is 32-bit signed, max 2^31-1; unsigned int max 2^32-1; long is 64-bit. 10^12 > 2^32, so 8-byte offsets are required. Arithmetic checked.

final_text: Average word length depends on what you count. In running text it is about 4.8 letters, because short words like 'the' repeat; across distinct words it is about 7.6 letters (Norvig's Google Books counts). A dictionary index stores distinct words, so the larger figure applies.
note: Norvig mayzner page: tokens 'The average is 4.79 letters per word'; distinct words 'Now the average is 7.60 letters long'. Both figures match.

final_text: S3 GetObject takes a standard HTTP Range header: for example, 'Range: bytes=0-9' returns only the first 10 bytes, and the response carries a Content-Range header. That call is what makes pointed reads into one big S3 object possible.
note: GetObject API: Range header 'Downloads the specified byte range of an object'; example 'Range: bytes=0-9' retrieves the first 10 bytes and returns 206 Partial Content. Page also says S3 'doesn't support retrieving multiple ranges of data per GET request' (see A-SSE-10).

final_text: A server can guard against reading a replaced file. It sends the ranged GET with If-Match set to the ETag its index was built from, and S3 returns 412 Precondition Failed instead of bytes if the object changed. The server can then reload its index rather than return garbage.
note: GetObject API, If-Match: 'Return the object only if its entity tag (ETag) is the same as the one specified in this header; otherwise, return a 412 Precondition Failed error.' Works with a ranged GET because it is a request-level precondition.

final_text: On S3, overwriting a key is atomic: a reader that races with the upload gets 'either the old data or the new data, but never partial or corrupt data'. The danger of a same-path upload is the stale index offsets, not a half-written file.
note: S3 user guide, consistency model: 'Updates to a single key are atomic ... you will get either the old data or the new data, but never partial or corrupt data.' Quote is verbatim.

final_text: A 1 TB dictionary cannot be uploaded in one request: a single S3 PUT is limited to 5 GB, so large files use multipart upload. As of October 2026, multipart allows up to 10,000 parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB each, and objects up to about 50 TB (48.8 TiB).
note: upload-objects page: single PUT 'up to 5 GB'; multipart 'up to 50 TB'. qfacts table: max object 48.8 TiB, 10,000 parts, part size 5 MiB to 5 GiB. All match as of 2026-10-13. (For 1 TB, 10,000 parts means parts of at least ~100 MB.)

final_text: Redis Pub/Sub is at-most-once: if a subscriber cannot handle a message, for example because of a network disconnect, 'the message is forever lost'. An API server that restarts at the wrong moment would miss the update event. Redis Streams persist messages if you need stronger delivery.
note: Redis Pub/Sub docs, Delivery semantics: 'at-most-once'; 'If the subscriber is unable to handle the message (for example, due to an error or a network disconnect) the message is forever lost.' Streams 'are persisted' with at-least-once support. Quote verbatim.

final_text: AWS says latency-sensitive applications can expect consistent S3 small-object (and first-byte) latencies of roughly 100-200 ms, and at least 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix. That is far slower than RAM, which is why AWS recommends a cache such as ElastiCache or CloudFront in front of S3 for hot data.
note: optimizing-performance page: 'at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE or 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned Amazon S3 prefix' (confirmed). Latency: the page says latency-sensitive applications 'can achieve consistent small object latencies (and first-byte-out latencies for larger objects) of roughly 100-200 milliseconds' - it is not a general 'S3 first-byte latency' figure, and the design-patterns page says small requests often have median latencies 'in the tens of milliseconds' (A-SSE-11). Reworded so the two additions do not conflict; caching advice is also on the page (CloudFront/ElastiCache).

final_text: SQLite is a real-world example of this portability: 'A database in SQLite is a single disk file'. The format is cross-platform, so a database created on one machine can be copied to and used on another architecture.
note: sqlite.org/onefile.html: 'A database in SQLite is a single disk file' (verbatim) and 'A database that is created on one machine can be copied and used on a different machine with a different architecture.'

final_text: The ZIP format itself is a one-file container with an index. A central directory near the end of the archive records, for every member, the offset of its local header, so a reader can seek straight to one file without unpacking the rest.
note: APPNOTE 6.3.9 (loaded): section 4.3.6 layout puts central directory headers and the end of central directory record at the end; 4.4.16 'relative offset of local header' gives each member's local header position.

final_text: Athena does not keep a row index for a CSV file; it scans the files a query touches and charges per TB scanned. To make queries cheaper and faster, compress the data, partition it, and convert it to a columnar format like Parquet so Athena reads only the needed columns.
note: Athena pricing page: '$5/TB' scanned example, GZIP '3:1 compression gains', Parquet so 'Athena only reads one-fourth of the file'. The pricing page does NOT mention partitioning; Athena docs (partitions.html) do: 'By partitioning your data, you can restrict the amount of data scanned by each query, thus improving performance and reducing cost.' Added that source. 'Does not index CSV rows' is an inference from scan billing, so softened.

final_text: AWS uses three storage terms. Block storage (Amazon EBS) is a disk-like volume attached to an instance. File storage (Amazon EFS) is a shared network file system, and object storage (Amazon S3) holds whole objects fetched over HTTP by key; the dictionary file on S3 is object storage.
note: AWS compare page: EBS 'block storage service'; EFS 'serverless, fully elastic file storage'; S3 'unlimited object storage'. Matches.

final_text: With S3 Versioning, each upload to the same key gets a unique version ID, and GetObject can request a specific version with the versionId parameter. Storing the version ID next to the path in meta.json would let every server keep reading exactly the version its index was built from.
note: S3 user guide: with versioning 'Amazon S3 generates a unique version ID for each object added'; GetObject: 'To return a different version, use the versionId subresource.' Requires s3:GetObjectVersion permission.

final_text: On AWS, an EC2 Auto Scaling instance refresh provides this out of the box. The rolling strategy replaces instances in batches, and with a minimum healthy percentage of 100 percent it launches new instances before terminating old ones, so capacity never drops.
note: Instance refresh overview: 'Rolling strategy (default) - Terminates instances and launches new ones in batches'; 'Launch the new instances first before terminating the old ones if the minimum healthy percentage is set to 100 percent.'

final_text: JSON Lines (one JSON value per line) is the usual fix when JSON must hold many records: it 'may be processed one record at a time', so readers stream it line by line instead of parsing one giant document. It still has no index, so a lookup is still a scan.
note: jsonlines.org: format 'may be processed one record at a time'; UTF-8, one JSON value per line. Quote verbatim.

final_text: A Lucene index is made of segments, each 'a fully independent index', plus a segments_N commit file. The optional compound format packs one segment's files into a single .cfs file.
note: Lucene 9.12 codec page: 'Each segment is a fully independent index, which could be searched separately'; segments_N 'Stores information about a commit point'; compound files 'collapsed into a single .cfs file'. Version drift: current Lucene is 10.5.2; its lucene104 codec page has the same three sentences, so I added it as the current source.

final_text: HDFS supports the same pointed read: its input streams offer seek() and positioned reads from a given byte offset. The offset-index design therefore also works on HDFS.
note: Hadoop FSDataInputStream spec: 'Callers may use Seekable.seek() to offsets within the array of bytes'; PositionedReadable read(position, buffer, offset, length). Spec covers Hadoop filesystems including HDFS.

final_text: Every PNG file begins with the same 8 bytes (hex 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A). The PNG specification says this signature 'differentiates a PNG datastream from other types of datastream and allows early detection of some transmission errors.'
note: PNG 3rd ed. 5.2: first eight bytes '89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A'; 'This signature differentiates a PNG datastream from other types of datastream and allows early detection of some transmission errors.' Quote matches.

final_text: A binary header must also fix the byte order of its integers. PNG stores all multi-byte integers in network byte order (most significant byte first), while Parquet stores its 4-byte metadata length little-endian; a decoder that assumes the wrong order reads garbage sizes.
note: PNG 7.1: 'All integers that require more than one byte shall be in network byte order', most significant byte first. Parquet: '4-byte length in bytes of file metadata (little endian)'. Both confirmed.

final_text: A Parquet file is laid out as 'PAR1', the column chunks, the file metadata, a 4-byte metadata length, and 'PAR1' again. Metadata is written after the data 'to allow for single pass writing', and readers first read it to find the column chunks they need.
note: Parquet file-format page: layout PAR1 / column chunks / File Metadata / 4-byte length / PAR1; 'to allow for single pass writing'; 'Readers are expected to first read the file metadata to find all the column chunks they are interested in.'

final_text: Putting the directory at the end is a common alternative to a header: a ZIP archive ends with its central directory and end-of-central-directory record, and MP4 muxers usually write the moov index at the end, with a 'faststart' pass that moves it to the beginning.
note: APPNOTE (cachefly copy is v6.3.10, Nov 2022) 4.3.6: central directory then end of central directory record at the end. ffmpeg-formats: MOV/MP4 index 'usually written at the end of the file'; faststart 'Run a second pass moving the index (moov atom) to the beginning of the file.'

final_text: RFC 4180 lets a CSV file have an optional first line of column names, and the text/csv MIME type has a 'header' parameter (present or absent) saying whether it is there. That header names columns; it does not say where data lies.
note: RFC 4180 rule 3: 'There maybe an optional header line appearing as the first line of the file'; MIME 'header' parameter 'Valid values are "present" or "absent"'.

final_text: As of October 2026, MDN lists Safari as the only browser that displays TIFF natively; other browsers need special libraries or add-ons, so TIFF is still avoided for web images.
note: MDN image types (2026-10-13): TIFF browser compatibility 'Safari'; 'Other than Safari, browsers do not natively support TIFF images in web content except by using special libraries or browser add-ons.'

final_text: NIST defines 1 MB as 10^6 bytes and 1 MiB as 2^20 = 1,048,576 bytes; for memory, 'megabyte' is often used for the binary size, so the two readings differ by about 5%.
note: NIST binary prefixes: '1 MiB = 2^20 B = 1 048 576 B'; '1 MB = 10^6 B'; 'When discussing computer memory, most manufacturers use megabyte to mean 2^20 = 1 048 576 bytes.' Difference 4.9% (about 5%).

final_text: The student's numbers come from real databases: PostgreSQL stores every table and index as fixed-size pages, usually 8 kB (PostgreSQL 18). Page-based B+ trees matter when an index is too big for RAM, which is not the case for this dictionary.
note: PostgreSQL 18.6 docs 66.6: 'Every table and index is stored as an array of pages of a fixed size (usually 8 kB ...)'. Second sentence is reasoning, fine for context.

final_text: AWS's Well-Architected Framework makes cost optimization one of its six pillars: a cost-optimized workload 'achieves an outcome at the lowest possible price point, and meets your functional requirements.'
note: Cost Optimization Pillar (June 27, 2024): 'A cost-optimized workload fully utilizes all resources, achieves an outcome at the lowest possible price point, and meets your functional requirements.' Quoted fragment is verbatim; framework 'based on six pillars'.

final_text: Real Bitcask writes a 'hint' file next to each data file holding just the keys and their positions. On startup it rebuilds the in-memory keydir from these small hint files instead of scanning the full data files, which shortens recovery a lot.
note: Riak KV 2.2.3 Bitcask docs: 'During startup, Bitcask will read from .hint files in order to build its in-memory representation of the key space', falling back to data files if hints are missing.

final_text: Riak's Bitcask defaults to sync_strategy = none, which writes data into operating-system buffers and leaves flushing to the OS, so a power or OS failure before the flush can lose recent writes. Setting o_sync forces a sync on every write, at a throughput cost.
note: Riak Bitcask docs: 'The default setting (none) writes data into operating system buffers'; 'o_sync - uses the O_SYNC flag, which forces syncs on every write.' The 'process crash loses nothing' clause is not on the page (true in principle, since data already sits in kernel buffers); reworded to stay within the source.

final_text: Riak's Bitcask rotates data files at max_file_size, 2 GB by default: when a write would push the active file past the limit, the file is closed and a new one opened.
note: Riak Bitcask docs: max_file_size 'The default is 2 GB'; when a write would exceed it the file is closed and a new one opened.

final_text: Riak's Bitcask triggers merges by how much garbage exists rather than on a fixed clock: by default a merge starts when a file has 60% dead keys or 512 MB of dead bytes, and files join a merge at 40% dead keys or 128 MB of dead bytes. A merge window can restrict merges to off-peak hours.
note: Riak Bitcask docs: fragmentation merge trigger 'default setting (60%)', dead bytes trigger 'The default is 512 MB'; thresholds 'default ratio (40%)' and 128 MB. Merge window settings (merge.window.start/end) restrict merging to chosen hours.

final_text: In Bitcask's source each entry is written as CRC32, timestamp, key size, value size, key, value, and the CRC32 is computed over everything after it. The reader decodes the same order and re-checks the CRC.
note: bitcask_fileops.erl write/4: Bytes0 = [Tstamp, KeySz, ValueSz, Key, Value]; Bytes = [crc32(Bytes0) | Bytes0]; read/3 re-computes crc32 over the bytes after the CRC and returns {error, bad_crc} on mismatch.

final_text: LevelDB's log format also starts each record with a CRC32C. When the reader finds corrupted data it skips it and resynchronises at the next block boundary rather than trying to repair it.
note: LevelDB log_format.md: record starts 'checksum: uint32 // crc32c of type and data[]'; 'If there is a corruption, skip to the next block.'

final_text: PostgreSQL protects each WAL record with a CRC-32C. The CRC is set when the record is written and checked during crash recovery, archive recovery and replication.
note: PG wal-reliability: 'Each individual record in a WAL file is protected by a CRC-32C (32-bit) check ... set when we write each WAL record and checked during crash recovery, archive recovery and replication.'

final_text: MySQL's binlog_checksum defaults to CRC32, so the server writes a checksum for each binary log event. The checksum is the last 4 bytes of the serialized event.
note: MySQL 8.4 refman: binlog_checksum 'The default is CRC32'; causes 'the source to write a checksum for each event'. Log_event_footer: checksum read at offset 'event length - BINLOG_CHECKSUM_LEN', i.e. trailing bytes; the page does not state the length, but a CRC32 is 4 bytes. Version drift: 8.4 is the LTS line; default unchanged.

final_text: PostgreSQL writes 8 KB pages, i.e. 16 sectors of 512 bytes, and a power loss can leave some sectors written and others not. To survive this it logs full page images to the WAL (full_page_writes), which can be turned off on file systems such as ZFS that prevent partial page writes.
note: PG wal-reliability: 'PostgreSQL typically writes 8192 bytes, or 16 sectors, at a time ... some of the 512-byte sectors were written while others were not'; full page images to WAL; 'If you have file-system software that prevents partial page writes (e.g., ZFS), you can turn off ... full_page_writes'.

final_text: S3 serves one byte range per GET (Range: bytes=start-end); it does not return multiple ranges in a single request. Concurrent ranged GETs are AWS's recommended way to download large objects quickly.
note: download-objects page: 'Amazon S3 doesn't support retrieving multiple ranges of data in a single GET request.' Design-patterns page: for large objects 'we suggest making concurrent requests ... by either requesting specific byte ranges'.

final_text: AWS says small S3 requests usually see median latencies in the tens of milliseconds, and recommends a cache (ElastiCache, CloudFront) in front of S3 for frequently read data.
note: Design-patterns page: for requests under 512 KB 'median latencies are often in the tens of milliseconds range'; cache section recommends CloudFront or ElastiCache for repeatedly requested objects.

final_text: An Apache Hudi index maps each record key (optionally with partition path) to the file id holding it. Bloom-filter and record-level indexes in the metadata table let upserts and point lookups avoid scanning every data file.
note: Hudi indexes page: index 'tracks a mapping from a given key (record key + optionally partition path) consistently to a file id'; bloom filters stored centrally in the metadata table; record index in record_index/ partition.

final_text: In Cassandra's write path every write goes first to the on-disk commit log, then to the in-memory memtable. Memtables are flushed to SSTables, which are immutable and never written again; with the default periodic commit-log sync (10 s) a crash can lose up to that window.
note: Cassandra storage-engine page (5.0 docs): commit log then memtable; 'SSTables are immutable, and never written to again after the memtable is flushed'; periodic commitlog_sync, default 10000 ms; 'can lose up to the sync period'.

final_text: In Riak each key is hashed onto a ring split into partitions owned by vnodes, and a write goes to the owning vnode and the vnodes for the next N-1 partitions. Any node can coordinate a request: there is no master node.
note: Riak clusters concept page: write goes 'to that vnode as well as to the vnodes responsible for the next N-1 partitions in the ring'; 'any node may participate as the coordinating node'. Why-Riak: 'There is no "master" node'.

final_text: Linux keeps file data that has been read in the page cache, so later reads of nearby bytes are served from memory without another disk access.
note: kernel.org mm concepts: 'Whenever a file is read, the data is put into the page cache to avoid expensive disk access on the subsequent reads.'

final_text: SQLite is the classic serverless engine: the application process reads and writes the database file directly, with no separate server process.
note: sqlite.org/serverless.html: 'the process that wants to access the database reads and writes directly from the database files on disk. There is no intermediary server process.'

final_text: Zoned storage devices, including zoned (ZNS) SSDs, require each zone to be written sequentially and reset before it can be rewritten; SSDs expose this interface to reduce write amplification. An append-only layout fits this model naturally.
note: zonedstorage.io: 'Zones in zoned storage devices must be written sequentially'; a zone 'must first be erased using a special command (zone reset)'; SSDs can 'implement a zoned interface in order to reduce write amplification'. The page does not call this 'a flash property' or say append-only layouts help; reworded so the last step is clearly our inference.
